case_name: State Bank of India & Ors. v. Manoj Kumar Das & Ors.
holding_summary: A three-judge Bench (CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana) declined to interfere with the NCLAT's 30 June 2026 order, which had affirmed NCLT Mumbai's direction that provident fund, gratuity and pension dues of former Jet Airways employees be paid in full and treated as falling outside the corporate debtor's liquidation estate. Lenders led by SBI had argued these dues should form part of the liquidation estate and be shared under the IBC waterfall unless a dedicated PF/gratuity fund existed at the commencement of liquidation. The Court found the lenders' points arguable but, given the peculiar facts of the case, declined to interfere, leaving the underlying legal questions open for a future case.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that employee provident fund, gratuity and pension dues can be treated as trust monies outside the liquidation waterfall even without a dedicated fund, which matters for resolution professionals, liquidators and secured lenders assessing recoveries in stressed-asset liquidations.

case_name: State of U.P. v. Jai Bir Singh
court: Supreme Court of India (Nine-Judge Constitution Bench)
holding_summary: A nine-judge Constitution Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant (with Justices B.V. Nagarathna, P.S. Narasimha, Dipankar Datta, Ujjal Bhuyan, Satish Chandra Sharma, Joymalya Bagchi, Alok Aradhe and Vipul M. Pancholi) revisited the 'triple test' for what constitutes an 'industry', laid down by the seven-judge bench in Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978). The Bench held that the 1978 triple test continues to govern industrial disputes still pending under the now-repealed Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, while refining aspects of that test, but held the 1978 ruling will no longer serve as the governing precedent ('sheet anchor') for disputes arising under the successor Industrial Relations Code.
why_it_matters: Ends decades of uncertainty over which establishments -- hospitals, educational bodies, government welfare departments, clubs -- qualify as an 'industry' for labour-dispute purposes, and narrows the expansive 1978 test's reach for future disputes; employers historically exposed under Bangalore Water Supply should reassess their position under the new Industrial Relations Code regime.

case_name: Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Union of India
holding_summary: The Supreme Court quashed a penalty for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax that had escalated from Rs. 12,000 in the original adjudication to Rs. 71,29,140 after the airline successfully appealed and secured a remand for de novo adjudication. Invoking the principle against 'reformatio in peius' -- that a litigant should not be placed in a worse position for having exercised a statutory right of appeal -- the Court held that mere delay in depositing tax already collected does not amount to 'failure to pay' attracting penalty under Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979, and directed refund of any penalty already paid, with 9% annual interest.
why_it_matters: Confirms that an appellate or remand process cannot be used to dramatically enhance a penalty beyond what was originally imposed, and clarifies that delayed remittance of tax already collected is legally distinct from non-payment -- relevant to any indirect-tax dispute where a taxpayer faces penalty escalation on remand.

case_name: Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that a financier's right of self-help repossession of a hypothecated vehicle cannot be exercised through force, deceit, or in breach of the loan agreement's terms, after Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company repossessed the appellant's commercial truck at 1 a.m. by breaking its steering lock without prior notice, following a loan default. The Court directed the financier to close the loan account, refund Rs. 4.5 lakh realised from the vehicle's sale with 6% annual interest, and pay Rs. 10 lakh compensation for mental agony and loss of livelihood, and separately directed RBI to ensure banks and NBFCs actually comply with its existing recovery and repossession guidelines, observing that those guidelines have 'existed only on paper'.
why_it_matters: Sharply raises the litigation and compensation exposure for banks and NBFCs (and their recovery agents) that repossess vehicles or other hypothecated assets without following RBI's fair-practice and due-process norms, and places RBI under a fresh judicial mandate to supervise actual compliance rather than merely issuing circulars.

case_name: National Highway Authority of India v. T. Younis & Anr.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that where a party files an application under Section 33 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 seeking correction, interpretation or an additional award, the three-month limitation period under Section 34(3) for challenging the award is reckoned from the date the arbitral tribunal disposes of that Section 33 application, regardless of whether the application is allowed or dismissed. The Court clarified that Section 34(3) does not distinguish between successful and unsuccessful Section 33 applications, but cautioned that where a Section 33 application is shown to be sham, frivolous or filed only to defeat limitation, courts may impose exemplary and punitive costs.
why_it_matters: Parties and counsel computing the limitation period for a Section 34 challenge after an unsuccessful Section 33 correction/clarification application now have clear Supreme Court authority that the clock still runs from the Section 33 disposal date, not the original award date, removing a recurring source of limitation disputes in arbitration challenges.

case_name: Union of India v. Sunil Biyani
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu held that no arrest can be effected under Section 69 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 for alleged tax evasion or fraud unless the order recording the officer's 'reasons to believe' for the arrest has first been communicated to the person concerned, including by electronic means such as registered email or the mobile number on record with the GST authorities. The Court also held that once a pre-arrest bail application is dismissed as not maintainable, a court cannot separately grant or extend interim protection from arrest, since that protection is ancillary to the pending application and cannot survive its dismissal.
why_it_matters: GST field formations must now communicate the Section 69 arrest order and its recorded reasons to the taxpayer before making an arrest, giving assessees a concrete procedural safeguard and a fresh window to seek anticipatory bail before any arrest is carried out.

case_name: Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC v. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta set aside the NCLAT's 2022 order and the CCI's 2021 order that had penalised Amazon Rs. 202 crore and purported to keep its already-approved 2019 investment in Future Coupons Private Limited 'in abeyance' over alleged suppression of facts in the merger notification. The Court held that once the CCI approves a combination under Section 31(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, it lacks statutory authority to keep that approval in abeyance or compel a fresh merger filing after the limitation period for review has expired. The CCI was directed to refund the penalty with 6% simple annual interest.
why_it_matters: Merging parties now have clearer assurance that a CCI approval of a combination is final and cannot later be suspended or reopened outside the Act's own review timelines merely on an allegation of incomplete disclosure, which matters for deal certainty in M&A and private equity transactions requiring CCI clearance.

case_name: Tata Steel Ltd. v. Varsha & Anr.
holding_summary: Arising from the Bhushan Steel Limited CIRP, the Supreme Court held that an operational creditor whose claim was admitted at a nominal quantified value of Re. 1 in an approved resolution plan cannot later revive the full, uncrystallised value of that claim through a pending civil suit or arbitration. The Court reaffirmed the 'clean slate' doctrine, holding that only claims crystallised and quantified as of the effective date of the resolution plan are payable on a pro-rata basis, and that claims not so crystallised stand abated, extinguished, waived or withdrawn once the plan is approved, dismissing both a pending civil recovery suit and connected arbitration references. The Court separately urged a legislative review of protections for MSME and other small operational creditors.
why_it_matters: Resolution applicants get further confirmation that the clean-slate principle protects them from stale, unquantified operational-creditor claims resurfacing years after a resolution plan takes effect, but operational creditors, especially MSMEs, are put on notice that they must ensure their claims are properly crystallised and quantified before the resolution plan is approved.

case_name: Rashmirekha Tripathy v. Sriram General Insurance Co. Ltd.
holding_summary: Laying down guidelines for assessing a deceased or injured claimant's income in motor accident compensation cases, the Supreme Court held that for salaried persons, the last available Income Tax Return ordinarily suffices to determine income, while for self-employed persons and business owners, tribunals should ordinarily take the average of up to three years' ITRs as the reference point for computing loss of dependency or loss of earning capacity.
why_it_matters: Motor Accident Claims Tribunals now have a clearer, standardised method for income assessment that reduces inconsistent approaches between salaried and self-employed claimants, narrowing the scope for disputes over quantum in future MACT claims.

case_name: Reliance General Insurance Company Limited v. Priyanka Das and Others
holding_summary: Deciding connected appeals arising from a single motorcycle-truck collision, the Supreme Court held, first, that the compensation multiplier for a deceased bachelor's death must be selected based on the deceased's own age under the standardised matrix in Sarla Verma and Pranay Sethi, not the age of the deceased's parents, applying multiplier 16 for the deceased's age bracket of 31-35 years. Second, on the injured pillion rider's claim, the Court held that functional earning capacity cannot be discounted merely because the claimant continued in the same employment role after the accident, enhancing her compensation to over Rs. 3.77 crore after she was certified as suffering 100% permanent disability, holding that earning capacity in the open labour market, not continued retention in a specific job, is the correct test.
why_it_matters: Confirms two claimant-favourable principles for MACT litigation: the age of the deceased (not the dependants') governs the multiplier for a bachelor's death, and continued employment post-accident does not by itself defeat a claim of substantial or total loss of future earning capacity.

case_name: The New India Assurance Company Limited & Ors. v. M/S Louis Dreyfus Commodities India Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: Ruling on a marine cargo turnover-based insurance policy where a fire caused losses exceeding the insured's declared annual turnover coverage, the Supreme Court held that Section 64VB of the Insurance Act, 1938 places an absolute embargo on an insurer assuming additional risk unless the corresponding premium is received in advance. Since the insured paid additional premium to cover the enhanced turnover only after the fire loss had already occurred, the Court held the insurer was not liable beyond the originally covered sum insured, and that an insurance agent's assurance of extended cover cannot override the statutory requirement of advance premium payment.
why_it_matters: Businesses operating turnover-linked or declaration-based insurance policies must ensure additional premium for enhanced coverage is paid before any loss event, not after; an agent's informal assurance of extended cover will not bind the insurer if Section 64VB's advance-premium requirement was not actually satisfied.

case_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sayona Colors Pvt. Ltd.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R. Mahadevan set aside a consumer commission award in favour of an insured that had claimed Rs. 28.2 crore for a 2011 godown fire, holding on forensic findings that the fire was the result of deliberate arson rather than an accidental short circuit, and that the claim coincided suspiciously with a recent enhancement of insurance coverage. The Court held that once fraud in an insurance claim is established, no relief, even partial, can be granted to the claimant, and directed constitution of a Special Investigation Team to probe the fraudulent claim.
why_it_matters: Confirms that Indian courts will not apportion 'partial genuine loss' relief once fraud is established in an insurance claim, and signals that egregious fraudulent claims can trigger criminal investigation via a court-ordered SIT even though the dispute originated as a civil consumer complaint.

case_name: Dr. Bais Surgical and Medical Institute Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. v. Dhananjay Pande
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Alok Aradhe held that an investor whose name was never entered in a company's register of members can nonetheless maintain a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, so long as the company's own conduct consistently recognised him as a stakeholder. On the facts, the respondent had invested substantial funds and was treated as Managing Director and 'co-owner', even though share certificates were never formally issued in his name; the Court held that formal non-entry in the statutory register could not defeat his substantive rights as a member.
why_it_matters: Companies cannot defeat a minority-oppression petition on the purely technical ground that the petitioner's name does not appear in the register of members where the company's own conduct, accepting investment, allotting a managerial role, treating the investor as a stakeholder, shows he was in substance a member; this closes off a common preliminary-objection strategy in oppression and mismanagement litigation.

case_name: M/s. GVV Constructions Private Limited v. The Union of India & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Alok Aradhe held that a High Court, exercising writ appellate jurisdiction, cannot pre-determine or constrain an Arbitral Tribunal's authority under Section 16 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to rule on its own jurisdiction. The dispute arose after South-Central Railway terminated a track-doubling contract with GVV Constructions; the Division Bench had directed the arbitrator to decide claims 'strictly in accordance with the terms of the contract,' which the Supreme Court found improperly circumscribed the Tribunal's inquiry into whether the termination fell within the contract's 'excepted matters' clause. The Court reaffirmed that such questions of arbitrability belong to the Tribunal under Section 16, not to a court exercising judicial review.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that government and infrastructure contractors litigating termination disputes under works contracts can expect the arbitral tribunal, not a writ court, to have the first and controlling word on whether a claim falls within an 'excepted matters' clause.

case_name: Sudhanshu Kardam v. Comptroller and Auditor General of India & Ors.
holding_summary: Two candidates with benchmark disabilities (specific learning disability and mental illness) who qualified in the SSC's Combined Graduate Level Examination, 2018 for the post of Auditor under the CAG were denied appointment because the post had not been identified as suitable for their disabilities under the older 2013 list. The Supreme Court held that a January 2021 Gazette notification under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 had superseded the 2013 list and expressly identified Auditor-category posts as suitable for these disabilities, so the candidates could not be denied appointment on the basis of the outdated list. The Court directed CAG to create supernumerary posts to accommodate both candidates.
why_it_matters: Public and private employers administering disability-reserved recruitment must apply the current RPwD Act identification notifications rather than older, superseded lists when assessing a candidate's eligibility for a reserved post.

case_name: ANI Media Pvt. Ltd. v. Open AI OpCo LLC & Ors.
holding_summary: Justice Amit Bansal dismissed news agency ANI's application for an interim injunction against OpenAI, which ANI alleged had trained ChatGPT on its copyrighted news content without authorisation. While accepting ANI's ownership of copyright in its content, the Court held that copyright protects only the original expression of a work and not the underlying facts, and found that using the content to train the model, together with the transformative nature of ChatGPT's outputs, weighed against a finding of infringement at the interim stage. The ruling is non-precedential (an interim order) and is under appeal before a Division Bench.
why_it_matters: India's first substantive judicial treatment of AI-model training against a copyright infringement claim; until the appeal is resolved, it is the leading (if non-binding) domestic guidance for how Indian courts may weigh fair-dealing/transformative-use arguments against content owners' claims over AI training data.

case_name: Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax & Anr. v. M/s. Omaxe Limited
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria held that once the Income Tax Settlement Commission passes a final order under Section 245D(4) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 determining an assessee's net taxable income, an Assessing Officer cannot invoke reassessment powers to reopen an issue already covered by that settlement. The dispute arose after the Department sought to reopen Omaxe Limited's ITSC-settled assessment to disallow a Rs. 65.65 crore deduction. The Court held Parliament had not envisaged reassessment as a route around a settlement order, and that the Revenue's only recourse, where it suspects fraud or misrepresentation in obtaining the settlement, is to approach the Settlement Commission itself under Section 245D(6).
why_it_matters: Gives finality to Income Tax Settlement Commission orders and closes off reassessment as a backdoor route for the Revenue to revisit issues an assessee has already settled, materially reducing reopening risk for taxpayers who have gone through ITSC proceedings.

case_name: Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited & Anr. v. Green Infra Wind Solutions Limited & Ors.
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Pamidighantam Sri Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar dismissed an appeal by Andhra Pradesh's power distribution companies and held that the Generation-Based Incentive (GBI), a Central government scheme benefit for wind power generators, is a distinct performance-linked payment to be disbursed to generating companies over and above the tariff fixed under their power purchase agreements. The Court held that while State Electricity Regulatory Commissions retain exclusive power to determine tariff and may factor in government grants generally, they cannot treat or adjust the GBI as part of the tariff itself, since doing so would defeat the incentive's purpose.
why_it_matters: Protects wind-energy generators' GBI revenue stream from being absorbed into, or set off against, DISCOM tariff payments, which matters for PPA structuring, project financing and revenue modelling in renewable energy transactions.

case_name: Reliance Eminent Trading and Commercial Private Limited v. Delhi Development Authority
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar laid down the first comprehensive, nine-point judicial framework for when a commercial court may grant summary judgment under Order XIII-A of the CPC (as applied through the Commercial Courts Act) without a full trial. Applying that framework, the Court found DDA's defences — on possession, non-joinder of the original owner, and limitation, in a dispute traced to a 2007 auction of a Jasola commercial plot whose underlying land acquisition had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the LARR Act — to be merely fanciful and not raising any real prospect of successfully resisting the claim. It set aside the 2008 conveyance deed under Article 142 and directed DDA to refund over Rs. 164 crore with 7.5% annual interest.
why_it_matters: Gives commercial courts and litigants the first authoritative checklist for seeking or resisting early disposal of commercial suits without a full trial, likely to speed up resolution of disputes where a defence has no real prospect of success.

case_name: Parle Products Pvt. Ltd. v. The Registrar of Trade Marks & Anr.
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices V. Kameswar Rao and Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora dismissed Parle's Letters Patent Appeal and affirmed registration of the '20-20' biscuit trademark in favour of Avon Agro, whose 'proposed to be used' application (filed 27 September 2007) predated Parle's own application by one week, even though Avon Agro never used the mark for 17 years while Parle built pan-India goodwill through continuous sales since 2007-08. The Court held that trademark priority under Section 18 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 is governed by the application filing date and cannot be defeated by a rival's later commercial use.
why_it_matters: Brand owners cannot assume that market goodwill or prior commercial use will trump a rival's earlier-filed 'proposed to be used' application; businesses must audit the register and oppose conflicting applications promptly rather than relying on established use as a fallback defence.

case_name: Kamlesh Rani Singla v. Praveen Kumar Garg & Anr.
citation: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 275 of 2026; 2026 LLBiz NCLAT 347
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: The NCLAT set aside Section 95 IBC insolvency proceedings initiated against Kamlesh Rani Singla, suspended director and personal guarantor of Laxmi Pipes Ltd., before NCLT New Delhi, holding that Section 60(2) of the IBC mandates such personal-guarantor proceedings be filed before the same NCLT bench (Chandigarh) where the corporate debtor's CIRP is pending, so NCLT New Delhi lacked both territorial and inherent jurisdiction. The Tribunal separately clarified that the NCLT President's power under Rule 16(d) to transfer cases between benches is not confined by territorial limits.
why_it_matters: Lenders and resolution professionals pursuing personal guarantors must file at the NCLT bench handling the corporate debtor's CIRP, not wherever is convenient; a wrong-bench filing risks being set aside for want of jurisdiction, delaying guarantor recovery actions.

case_name: Hotel Alankar v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices Sharmila U. Deshmukh and Neeraj P. Dhote quashed the appellate authority's order and revoked the suspension of a Karad hotel's FSSAI licence, holding that licence suspension under Section 32 of the Food Safety and Standards Act exists to protect public health and cannot be continued indefinitely once the establishment rectifies deficiencies and achieves 'exemplar' compliance (97%, i.e. 106/110) on re-inspection. The Court held that any penalty for sales made during the suspension period must instead be pursued separately under Sections 55 and 63 of the Act.
why_it_matters: Food businesses facing an FSSAI licence suspension now have clear appellate authority that demonstrated, verified compliance on re-inspection should end the suspension promptly, preventing regulators from using continued suspension as an unstated additional penalty.

case_name: Raj Karan Singh v. Union of India & Ors.
citation: Civil Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 14490 of 2024; 2026 LLBiz HC(PAT) 25
holding_summary: Justice Girijish Kumar held that Tata Motors Finance Ltd. could not treat an ex parte arbitral award as self-executing to seize a defaulting borrower's commercial truck; under Section 36 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an arbitral award must be enforced as a civil court decree through the competent court's execution process, not through unilateral self-help repossession. Finding the financier had 'taken the law in its own hand,' the Court directed compensation equal to the vehicle's insurance value on the date of seizure, to be adjusted against the outstanding loan.
why_it_matters: Financiers holding an arbitral award against a defaulting borrower cannot bypass Section 36 execution proceedings to directly repossess secured assets; they must obtain a formal execution order, materially raising the litigation and compliance risk of self-help enforcement.

case_name: HDFC Bank Ltd. v. Thomas Alexander
holding_summary: A Single Member Bench (Saroj Yadav, Presiding Member) allowed HDFC Bank's revision petition and held that its written statement, filed after the complaint copy was received on 24 September 2025, fell within the maximum permissible 45-day period (30 days extendable by 15 for sufficient cause) under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The Commission set aside the State Commission's order that had refused to condone delay and struck the written statement off the record.
why_it_matters: Confirms the 45-day outer limit for filing a written statement in consumer proceedings is an absolute, sacrosanct ceiling rather than one State Commissions can shorten through strict practice, giving respondents -- including banks and other regulated entities -- a clear, enforceable procedural safeguard.

case_name: Omaxe Ltd. v. Asha Saini
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices V. Kameswar Rao and Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora dismissed Omaxe's Section 37 appeals against a Commercial Court order upholding two arbitral awards granting homebuyer Asha Saini 15% per annum compensation for delayed possession of two flats booked in 2006 in Omaxe's 'Omaxe North Avenue' project, Bahadurgarh. The Court rejected Omaxe's argument that a homebuyer who chose arbitration has fewer substantive rights than one proceeding under RERA or the Consumer Protection Act, and imposed Rs. 1 lakh costs on each appeal.
why_it_matters: Confirms homebuyers pursuing delay-compensation claims through arbitration under a builder-buyer agreement's arbitration clause are not disadvantaged compared to those using RERA or consumer fora, so arbitral awards in builder-buyer disputes will receive the same appellate deference.

case_name: In re: Scheme of Amalgamation of Mawana Foods Pvt. Ltd. with Mawana Sugars Ltd.
citation: NCLT New Delhi order dated 3 September 2026, under Sections 230-232, Companies Act, 2013
court: National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi Bench
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Members Manni Sankariah Shanmuga Sundaram (Judicial) and Reena Sinha Puri (Technical) sanctioned the scheme of amalgamation of wholly-owned subsidiary Mawana Foods Pvt. Ltd. into its parent, Mawana Sugars Ltd., holding the scheme was not prejudicial to the interests of shareholders or creditors of either company. Because Mawana Foods is wholly owned, the scheme involves no fresh share issuance and the transferee's authorised capital remains unchanged.
why_it_matters: Illustrates the streamlined NCLT approval path available for wholly-owned-subsidiary mergers where no share exchange ratio is needed, offering a practical template for corporate groups seeking to simplify structure and cut duplication through intra-group amalgamation.

case_name: Samaj Parivartana Samudaya & Ors. v. State of Karnataka & Ors.
citation: Order dated 8 September 2026 in W.P.(C) No. 562 of 2009
holding_summary: A Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana permitted Karnataka to auction and lease composite mining blocks that include parcels of 'virgin forest land,' as an 'operational rationalisation' allowing adjoining parcels to be planned and auctioned as a single mine, on condition the successful bidder cannot commence mining on the virgin-forest portion until forest-clearance approval is separately obtained. The Court also permitted conditional sale of minerals from expired mining leases subject to safeguards, and listed the matter for further orders on 29 September 2026.
why_it_matters: Lets mining companies bid for and financially commit to composite blocks containing forest land before forest clearance is secured, easing auction and project-planning timelines while keeping environmental clearance intact as a precondition to actual mining -- relevant to bidders, lenders and environmental counsel structuring mining-block acquisitions.

case_name: 3S and Our Health Society v. Union of India & Anr.
citation: Miscellaneous Application No. 1177 of 2025 in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 437 of 2024
holding_summary: Hearing a public interest litigation on packaged-food labelling, a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran examined FSSAI's affidavit (dated 28 August 2026) proposing a phased front-of-pack labelling (FoPL) regime using a red hexagonal warning symbol for products high in added sugar, salt or saturated fat, based on thresholds in the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024. The Court found FSSAI's proposal broadly acceptable in principle but identified over a dozen unresolved gaps - including implementation timelines, nutrient thresholds and consumer comprehension - and directed the Centre and FSSAI to file a clarificatory affidavit within ten days, with the matter listed for further hearing on 28 September 2026.
why_it_matters: A mandatory red-hexagon front-of-pack warning label regime, once finalised, would require packaged-food manufacturers and FBOs across India to redesign labelling and reformulate or reclassify products exceeding the notified sugar/salt/fat thresholds - businesses in the food and FMCG sector should track the 28 September hearing and the FSSAI affidavit for the proposed compliance timeline.

case_name: Satya Prakash Bagla & Anr. v. Kanta Agarwala & Ors.
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
holding_summary: The NCLAT dismissed appeals against an NCLT order that had found oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of Exclusive Capital Limited, an RBI-registered NBFC. Between October 2021 and March 2022, Teesta Retail Pvt. Ltd. invested Rs. 315 crore in the company through Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) against owned funds of only about Rs. 2.34 crore, pushing the company's leverage ratio to roughly 117.77 against RBI's prescribed ceiling of 7 (for which RBI separately imposed a Rs. 10.30 lakh penalty). The subsequent conversion of these OCDs into Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares, combined with other governance failures, was held by the NCLT and affirmed by the NCLAT to constitute oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013, justifying NCLT's continued interference in the company's affairs.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a massive breach of RBI leverage/capital-adequacy norms by an NBFC, combined with debt-to-equity instrument conversions that dilute or disadvantage existing stakeholders, can itself furnish grounds for an oppression-and-mismanagement petition - relevant for NBFC promoters, investors and minority shareholders assessing governance risk in group companies.

case_name: Muthoot Finance Ltd. (Informant) v. Trustees' Association of India, IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd., Axis Trustee Services Ltd. & SBICAP Trustee Company Ltd.
citation: Competition Commission of India, order dated 02.09.2026
holding_summary: The CCI held that the Trustees' Association of India (TAI) and three major debenture trustees -- IDBI Trusteeship Services, Axis Trustee Services and SBICAP Trustee Company -- violated Sections 3(3)(a) and 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act, 2002 by collectively fixing a minimum benchmark fee for debenture trusteeship services during FY 2020-21 and FY 2021-22, after TAI decided in March 2021 that members would not price below a common floor and monitored quotations to enforce it. The complaint was triggered by Muthoot Finance after its long-standing trustee quoted a sharply higher fee for a proposed NCD issuance. The Commission issued a cease-and-desist order but imposed no monetary penalty, noting the trustees had abandoned the benchmark-alignment practice once the investigation began, while warning that any recurrence would be treated as aggravated recidivism.
why_it_matters: Confirms that professional/intermediary trade associations in India's debt-capital-markets ecosystem can be held liable for price-fixing under the Competition Act even absent a formal cartel agreement, and signals to issuers and trustees that association-driven fee benchmarking carries real antitrust exposure despite the no-penalty outcome here.

case_name: Rani Gupta v. Management Committee, Maheshwari Public School & Anr.
citation: Rajasthan High Court (Jaipur Bench), order dated August 2026
holding_summary: Justice Anuroop Singhi enhanced compensation payable to a Hindi teacher, illegally terminated in 2015 after roughly 20 years of unblemished service on the ground that there were no students for Hindi, from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 20 lakh. The Rajasthan Non-Government Educational Institutions Tribunal had found the termination bad in law but, since the teacher had since reached superannuation, awarded only Rs. 1 lakh in lieu of reinstatement; the High Court called that amount 'shockingly disproportionate' given her permanent status, clean service record, and the 67-plus months she remained without employment before superannuation, and directed payment of Rs. 20 lakh within two months.
why_it_matters: Signals that Rajasthan courts will substantially scale up lump-sum compensation in lieu of reinstatement for long-serving private-school and institutional employees found to be illegally terminated, raising the litigation exposure for educational trusts and other non-government institutional employers on wrongful termination claims.

case_name: Arun Kumar Singh v. Genius Exports Private Limited & Ors.
citation: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1699, 1700, 1701 & 1702 of 2025, NCLAT New Delhi
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi (Principal Bench)
holding_summary: The NCLAT held that the death of a successful/settling resolution applicant before formal approval of a resolution plan does not, by itself, justify liquidation of the corporate debtor -- particularly where a Section 12A withdrawal application based on an underlying settlement remained pending before the Adjudicating Authority. The Tribunal set aside the NCLT's liquidation order dated 17 September 2025, revived the CIRP of Genius Exports Pvt. Ltd., and directed the NCLT to take up and decide the pending Section 12A withdrawal application on its merits.
why_it_matters: Gives resolution professionals, creditors and settling parties clarity that the death of an individual applicant or promoter mid-process is not an automatic trigger for liquidation, preserving the possibility of a negotiated exit or revived resolution even after such an intervening event.

case_name: Energy Beverages Pvt. Ltd. v. Sabran Enterprises & Ors.
citation: Interim Application (L) No. 12425 of 2026 in Commercial IP Suit (L) No. 11510 of 2026, Bombay High Court
holding_summary: Justice Madhav J. Jamdar restrained a Karnataka-based business from manufacturing or selling packaged drinking water under the 'CLEAR/CLEAR AQUA IND' mark, after physically comparing the rival products at an earlier hearing and finding them prima facie counterfeit -- with identical bottle shapes, label design, colour scheme and feature placement, and 'AQUA IND' rendered in negligible font while 'CLEAR' was given disproportionate prominence. The interim order followed Energy Beverages' claims of trademark infringement, copyright infringement of its label artwork, and passing off.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that courts will readily grant interim injunctions against close packaging/get-up copying in the FMCG and packaged-water sector where side-by-side comparison shows deliberate imitation, a useful precedent for brand owners pursuing fast interim relief against counterfeit look-alikes.

case_name: Premium Sugars v. Union of India & Ors.
citation: Writ Petition (L) No. 18701 of 2026, Bombay High Court
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices Suman Shyam and Advait M. Sethna dismissed a batch of petitions by merchant sugar exporters challenging the DGFT's 13 May 2026 notification that changed sugar's export status from 'Restricted' to 'Prohibited' until 30 September 2026. The exporters, who held pre-existing private contracts and had received full advance payment from overseas buyers between 14 April and 4 May 2026, argued the ban retrospectively defeated vested and legitimate expectation rights; the Court held that private bilateral contracts and advance payments do not confer a legal right capable of overriding a subsequent statutory export policy issued under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 in the larger public interest, invoking the maxim salus populi est suprema lex.
why_it_matters: Confirms that exporters cannot rely on already-executed private sale contracts or advance payments to resist a subsequent government export restriction on an essential commodity, an important risk allocation point for trading houses and commodity exporters structuring cross-border sugar and other agri-commodity contracts.

case_name: State of Haryana & Ors. v. M/s Faridabad Gurgaon Minerals & Anr. (with State of Haryana & Ors. v. M/s Ganpati Enterprises Slate Mines)
holding_summary: A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma held that a mining lessee cannot claim a vested right to pay a static royalty or dead rent for the entire lease term merely because the lease deed is silent on revision, where the State's statutory power to revise such levies flows independently from Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and rules made thereunder. The Court set aside a 2016 Punjab and Haryana High Court judgment that had quashed a Haryana government notification enhancing royalty and dead rent on minor-mineral leases originally auctioned in 2001, allowing the State's appeals.
why_it_matters: Confirms that mining lessees across India cannot rely on silence in a lease deed to resist statutory royalty revisions, giving state governments a strong precedent to enforce revised royalty and dead-rent notifications against minor-mineral and other lessees mid-lease.
